title: Arabic Feature's Activation Mass
takeaway: Re-weighting the feature's activation histogram by activation magnitude shows that almost all of the total activation the Arabic script feature contributes comes from tokens the proxy scores as Arabic. The weak, less pure activations that dominate the raw token counts contribute almost nothing once weighted, which is the paper's case that the feature is specific in the way that matters.
walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

This is one chart about one [[feature]]: the [[arabic-script-feature]], written A/1/3450 in the paper's [[feature-notation]].

The horizontal axis is the level at which that feature fires on a token, running from just above zero out to 9.

The vertical axis is not a count of tokens. Each bin's height is the total activation the tokens in that bin contribute: roughly how many tokens landed there, multiplied by how hard the feature fired on them. Frequency times magnitude is an expected value, which is where the name comes from. The paper calls this an [[expected-value-plot]] and takes the device from Cammarata et al.'s curve detector work.

The fill is split by color. Red is tokens the [[arabic-script-proxy]] scores as Arabic; blue is tokens it scores as not Arabic. The color scale is printed on the companion [[feature-activation-distribution-plot]], not here.

### How to read it

Put the two charts side by side at one x position. Near an activation of 6.9 the plain density plot sits at about 4.7 thousand tokens. Multiply 4.7 thousand by 6.9 and you get roughly 32 thousand, which is where this chart peaks.

Now do the same at the far left. There the density plot is at its tallest, above 5 thousand tokens, but the activation level is near zero. The product is near zero, so that whole region flattens here.

That is the mechanism: the left edge, where the blue non-Arabic sliver is proportionally widest, is exactly the region this weighting shrinks.

### What it shows

Red covers nearly all the area under the curve. So most of the activation magnitude this feature supplies comes from Arabic-script contexts, even though the unweighted counts at weak activations looked much less clean — only 25% Arabic at the very bottom of the range.

The paper's reason for calling this the honest view is [[large-activations-dominate]]: in a one-layer transformer, features act on the logits approximately linearly, so a bigger activation has a bigger effect. It flags that this argument is solid for a one-layer model and rests on conjecture for larger ones.

The plot does not adjudicate between the three [[weak-activation-hypotheses]]. It argues instead that whichever explains the weak blue tail, that tail carries little weight.

terms.definition: The name of this plot: the distribution of the feature's activations, with each bin weighted by activation level rather than counted once per token. It answers "where does this feature's total activation come from" rather than "where does it fire most often".

The identifier of the feature being plotted. Under the paper's scheme the first part names the transformer ("A", the main one-layer model), the second the dictionary learning run (run 1), and the third the index of the feature within that run (3450).

The vertical quantity: activation level multiplied by how many tokens fell in that bin, summed within the bin. It is total activation mass in the sampled data, not a token count, and its units depend on how much data was sampled.
The scalar value the feature takes on a token, i.e. the post-ReLU coefficient the sparse autoencoder assigns to this feature's direction. Larger means the feature fired harder.

A marker separating tokens with strictly positive activation from hard zeros. The sparsity penalty drives most activations to exactly zero, which would put a spike at the origin, so exact zeros are excluded from the plotted curve.
The share of each bin's activation mass coming from tokens whose surrounding string the Arabic proxy scores as Arabic script (a high log-likelihood ratio).
The share of each bin's activation mass coming from tokens the proxy scores as not Arabic (a low log-likelihood ratio). It appears here as a thin band along the top of the red.

terms.term: Log-Likelihood Ratio (color scale, inherited from the companion plot)
terms.definition: The score coloring the fill, $\log(P(s|\text{Arabic Script}) / P(s))$: how much more likely the string is under the hypothesis that it is Arabic than under the general data distribution. This chart reuses the scale printed on the preceding density plot rather than repeating it.
A cheaply computable score standing in for the hypothesis about what a feature detects, used as an independent yardstick so the paper is not just eyeballing its own examples.
The claim this figure supports: that the feature being on implies the hypothesized context is present. It is the half of the case against polysemanticity that the paper treats as more important.
The two colors are stacked, not overlaid, so the outer outline is the total activation mass at that activation level and the internal boundary splits it into Arabic and non-Arabic parts.

numbers.meaning: The y-axis ticks, in thousands of units of activation mass. The scale is set by the size of the sampled dataset, so the absolute values carry no meaning on their own; only the shape and the red/blue split are read off this chart.
The x-axis ticks in activation level. 9 is roughly the largest activation this feature reaches, and the curve is already at the floor well before it.

numbers.value: about 32.5K, at an activation of roughly 6.9
numbers.meaning: The peak of the curve. This is where frequency and magnitude multiply best: the companion density plot has a local peak of about 4.7 thousand tokens there, and 4.7K times 6.9 is about 32K.

Tokens with barely positive activations are the most numerous, above 5 thousand in the density plot, but multiplying that count by an activation near zero leaves almost no mass. This is the whole point of the re-weighting.
A mid-range reading: moderate counts times moderate activations still give only about a sixth of the peak's mass.

numbers.value: falls to the floor between 8.0 and 8.5
numbers.meaning: Above about 8 the feature almost never fires, so however large the multiplier, there is nearly nothing to multiply.

The share of training tokens that are Arabic script, per the paper's proxy. It is the base rate this figure is implicitly compared against — Arabic is rare in the data, so a mostly-red chart is a strong statement.

The share of tokens on which the feature is active at all that the proxy scores as Arabic, counting each active token once. This figure's magnitude-weighted version of the same question comes out higher.
The Arabic share when the feature is barely active. This is the impure region, and it is the region this plot's weighting shrinks to nearly nothing.
The Arabic share when activation is above 5. Because these strong activations carry most of the mass, they dominate the red area here.

The range of the log-likelihood ratio color scale on the companion plot, which this chart's colors follow. Deep blue is a string five nats less likely under the Arabic hypothesis than under the general distribution; deep red is five nats more likely.

The probability the proxy assigns to $P(\text{Arabic}|s)$ when the string contains any non-Arabic character. It is what makes punctuation, whitespace and split byte-tokens score as strongly non-Arabic, and so is one source of the blue that survives at high activations.
The Unicode blocks the proxy treats as Arabic script. Characters outside them count as non-Arabic even when they appear inside Arabic text, which is why the paper calls the proxy imperfect.

The paper's example of a single Arabic character split into two byte-level tokens. The feature typically fires only on the second token of such a pair, which affects where mass lands along the x-axis.

The depth of the transformer being studied. It is what makes the argument behind this plot — that larger activations have larger effects, because features hit the logits approximately linearly — hold firmly here and only conjecturally in deeper models.
